WITH per_req AS (
  SELECT r.request_id, r.city,
         MIN(e.event_ts) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'MATCHED')              AS first_match,
         COUNT(DISTINCT e.driver_id) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'MATCHED')  AS drivers,
         COALESCE(BOOL_OR(e.event_type = 'PICKED_UP'), false)                 AS picked_up
  FROM trip_requests r
  JOIN dispatch_events e ON e.request_id = r.request_id
  GROUP BY r.request_id, r.city
), last_cancel AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (request_id) request_id, party, event_ts
  FROM dispatch_events
  WHERE event_type = 'CANCELLED'
  ORDER BY request_id, event_ts DESC, event_id DESC
), lost AS (
  SELECT p.city, c.party,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM c.event_ts - p.first_match)::bigint AS wait_s,
         p.drivers >= 2                                          AS rematched
  FROM per_req p
  JOIN last_cancel c ON c.request_id = p.request_id
  WHERE p.first_match IS NOT NULL
    AND NOT p.picked_up
), bucketed AS (
  SELECT l.*,
         CASE WHEN wait_s < {{b1_s}} THEN 1
              WHEN wait_s < {{b2_s}} THEN 2
              ELSE 3 END AS bucket_no
  FROM lost l
)
SELECT city,
       party AS cancelled_by,
       CASE bucket_no WHEN 1 THEN '{{bucket_a}}' WHEN 2 THEN '{{bucket_b}}' ELSE '{{bucket_c}}' END AS wait_bucket,
       COUNT(*)                            AS lost_requests,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rematched)   AS rematched_requests,
       MAX(wait_s)                         AS max_wait_s
FROM bucketed
GROUP BY city, party, bucket_no
ORDER BY city, cancelled_by, bucket_no;

Explanation. Everything hinges on the grain. First reduce the events to one row per request: the first match time (MIN … FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'MATCHED')), the number of distinct drivers matched, and whether the rider was ever picked up. Separately, DISTINCT ON with event_ts DESC, event_id DESC picks each request's last cancellation, which decides the party. The inner join between the two keeps only requests that were cancelled; the WHERE keeps those that were matched and never picked up, which removes both cancellations before a match and driver cancellations that were rescued by a re-match. The wait is measured from the first match, so a re-match does not reset the rider's clock. The bucket is a number for grouping and ordering, and the label is derived from it, so '10m+' can never sort before '2-5m'.

Complexity. One aggregate pass and one sort for DISTINCT ON, both by request: O(n log n) over events. At marketplace scale both steps are local to a request, so partitioning events by request (or by request date with a small spill-over) keeps it a single shuffle.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: no DISTINCT ON; use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY request_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC) = 1, COUNTIF, MIN(IF(event_type = 'MATCHED', event_ts, NULL)), LOGICAL_OR, and TIMESTAMP_DIFF(…, SECOND). Snowflake: QUALIFY, COUNT_IF, BOOLOR_AGG, DATEDIFF('second', …); COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(event_type = 'MATCHED', driver_id, NULL)). Spark SQL: max_by(party, struct(event_ts, event_id)) picks the last cancellation in one aggregate; count(DISTINCT CASE …). MySQL 8: no FILTER or DISTINCT ON; use CASE inside aggregates and ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE, TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …).

Edge cases built into the data. Waits of exactly {{b1_s}} and {{b2_s}} seconds; requests cancelled before any match; driver cancellations rescued by a re-match and completed; lost trips with a re-match. Hard: system cancellations after a driver cancelled and nobody accepted; riders cancelling while dispatch was re-matching; a driver and a rider cancellation in the same second (the higher event_id is last). Very Hard: late uploads, so event_id order differs from time order (one request's last cancellation was ingested before an earlier one); a MATCHED row and a CANCELLED row duplicated by client retries.

Common mistakes. Counting events instead of requests; measuring from the latest match; including cancellations before a match or rescued driver cancellations; ordering by event_id alone; counting re-matches from MATCHED rows instead of distinct drivers; <= at a bucket edge; ordering by the label text; an INNER JOIN that is fine here but a LEFT JOIN that leaves pre-match cancellations with a NULL wait in some bucket.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A rider-cancellation rate divides by matched requests (every matched rider could cancel); a driver-cancellation rate is best per match (every match is a chance for that driver), so a re-matched request contributes several driver denominators. (2) Classify each lost trip by whether its last cancellation fell within the grace period from the match that was current then (or from the first match, stated explicitly); one bucket per request still. (3) Key the daily table by request and recompute any request touched by a late event (a merge on request_id); declare a day final after a lateness bound, and publish restatements with a version. (4) Partition by event date and cluster by request; a request spanning midnight needs its events from both days, so compute from a two-day read or partition by request date instead of event date.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but events counted instead of requests, or the clock reset on re-match. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also gives the right rate denominators and a credible late-data design.

Strong signals. States the grain ("one row per request") before writing SQL; asks whether a re-match resets the wait; orders buckets by rank. Red flags. COUNT(*) over joined events; treating event_id as time.

WITH spans AS (
  SELECT d.city, s.driver_id, s.status, s.changed_at AS started,
         LEAST(COALESCE(LEAD(s.changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY s.driver_id ORDER BY s.changed_at, s.event_id),
                        TIMESTAMPTZ '{{to_ts}}'),
               s.changed_at + make_interval(secs => {{cap_s}})) AS ended
  FROM driver_status s
  JOIN drivers d ON d.driver_id = s.driver_id
), online AS (
  SELECT city, driver_id, status,
         GREATEST(started, TIMESTAMPTZ '{{from_ts}}') AS a,
         LEAST(ended, TIMESTAMPTZ '{{to_ts}}')        AS b
  FROM spans
  WHERE status IN ('OPEN', 'EN_ROUTE', 'ON_TRIP')
), hours AS (
  SELECT h FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMPTZ '{{from_ts}}', TIMESTAMPTZ '{{to_ts}}' - INTERVAL '1 hour', INTERVAL '1 hour') AS g(h)
), pieces AS (
  SELECT o.city, h.h AS hour_start, o.driver_id, o.status,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM LEAST(o.b, h.h + INTERVAL '1 hour') - GREATEST(o.a, h.h)) AS secs
  FROM online o
  JOIN hours h ON o.a < h.h + INTERVAL '1 hour' AND o.b > h.h
  WHERE o.a < o.b
), per_hour AS (
  SELECT city, hour_start,
         COUNT(DISTINCT driver_id)                                  AS drivers,
         COALESCE(SUM(secs) FILTER (WHERE status = 'OPEN'), 0)      AS open_s,
         COALESCE(SUM(secs) FILTER (WHERE status = 'EN_ROUTE'), 0)  AS en_route_s,
         COALESCE(SUM(secs) FILTER (WHERE status = 'ON_TRIP'), 0)   AS on_trip_s
  FROM pieces
  GROUP BY city, hour_start
)
SELECT city, hour_start, drivers,
       ROUND(open_s / 60.0, 2)     AS open_min,
       ROUND(en_route_s / 60.0, 2) AS en_route_min,
       ROUND(on_trip_s / 60.0, 2)  AS on_trip_min,
       ROUND(on_trip_s / (open_s + en_route_s + on_trip_s), 4) AS utilisation
FROM per_hour
ORDER BY city, hour_start;

Explanation. A change table becomes spans with LEAD over the driver's rows in (changed_at, event_id) order; the last row has no successor, so it runs to the window end (and, at Very Hard, no longer than the cap after its own row). Rows from before the window are kept on purpose: the last of them is the status in effect when the window opens, and clipping with GREATEST/LEAST turns it into the window's first minutes. Rows after the window produce spans that clip to nothing. The hour split is an interval join between each clipped span and the window's hours from generate_series, keeping LEAST(end, hour end) − GREATEST(start, hour start). Seconds are summed per status with FILTER, and only the final columns are divided and rounded.

Complexity. One sort by driver for the window function, then a join whose output is about (spans × hours each span touches), which is close to the number of spans: O(n log n). The WHERE o.a < o.b filter matters: without it, spans clipped to nothing still satisfy the overlap test and produce negative seconds.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: GENERATE_TIMESTAMP_ARRAY(from, to, INTERVAL 1 HOUR) with UNNEST; TIMESTAMP_DIFF(…, SECOND); COUNTIF/SUM(IF(…)); TIMESTAMP_ADD(changed_at, INTERVAL cap SECOND). Snowflake: a generator or calendar table for hours, DATEDIFF('second', …), DATEADD, IFF. Spark SQL: sequence(from, to, interval 1 hour) + explode, unix_timestamp differences. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE for the hours, TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …), SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Statuses crossing hour boundaries; a change exactly on an hour boundary (no sliver on the other side). Hard: drivers online before the window opens; drivers still online when it closes, one of them with no later row at all; OFFLINE rows after the window; two rows of one driver in the same second (the lower event_id lasts zero seconds). Very Hard: repeated same-status rows while the app runs, silences longer than the cap whose remainder must not count, and late uploads so event_id is not time order.

Common mistakes. Crediting a whole span to the hour it started; filtering changed_at to the window and so losing the status in effect at the start; giving the last status no duration, or extending it past the window; ordering by changed_at alone; counting status rows as drivers; rounding minutes before computing utilisation; dividing by all time including OFFLINE; ignoring the cap at Very Hard.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Utilisation alone does not show oversupply: look at request wait times (ETAs), unfulfilled requests, EN_ROUTE share (long pickups), and earnings per online hour; a city with short trips and long pickups can show low utilisation and still be undersupplied. (2) Decide a product-neutral definition (online if online for any product) and attribute trips to the product that was on board; never sum per-product online time. (3) Keep each driver's current status and its start time as state; every hour, close the hour for each online driver and emit their seconds, plus spans from the hour's changes. (4) Publish provisionally after a short delay, finalise after a lateness bound (for example 24 hours), and restate by recomputing the drivers touched by late rows.

Rubric anchors. 2: right spans but no hour split, or the carried-in status lost. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also reasons well about what utilisation means and about incremental computation.

Strong signals. Draws a timeline for one driver across an hour boundary and the window edges before coding; filters spans that clip to nothing. Red flags. SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM …)) over rows grouped by date_trunc('hour', changed_at); assuming every driver starts the window offline.

WITH first_pickup AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id) order_id, courier_id, event_ts AS picked_at
  FROM courier_events
  WHERE event_type = 'PICKED_UP'
  ORDER BY order_id, event_ts, event_id
), measured AS (
  SELECT p.order_id, o.merchant_id, m.time_zone, p.picked_at,
         MIN(a.event_ts) AS arrived_at
  FROM first_pickup p
  JOIN delivery_orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
  JOIN merchants m       ON m.merchant_id = o.merchant_id
  JOIN courier_events a  ON a.order_id = p.order_id
                        AND a.courier_id = p.courier_id
                        AND a.event_type = 'ARRIVED'
                        AND a.event_ts <= p.picked_at
  GROUP BY p.order_id, o.merchant_id, m.time_zone, p.picked_at
), labelled AS (
  SELECT merchant_id,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM picked_at - arrived_at) AS wait_s,
         CASE
           WHEN EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) >= 6
            AND EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) < 11 THEN 1
           WHEN EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) < 6  THEN 5
           WHEN EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) < 15 THEN 2
           WHEN EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) < 17 THEN 3
           WHEN EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) < 22 THEN 4
           ELSE 5
         END AS part_no
  FROM measured
)
SELECT merchant_id,
       (ARRAY['breakfast', 'lunch', 'afternoon', 'dinner', 'late_night'])[part_no] AS daypart,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE wait_s > {{n_s}})     AS long_waits,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE wait_s > {{n_s}}) / COUNT(*), 1) AS long_wait_pct,
       MAX(wait_s)                                  AS max_wait_s
FROM labelled
GROUP BY merchant_id, part_no
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_orders}}
ORDER BY merchant_id, part_no;

Explanation. The pickup decides everything, so pick it first: the earliest PICKED_UP row per order (a retried row comes later and is ignored), and its courier. Only that courier waited, so the arrival join is restricted to the same courier_id, to ARRIVED events, and to times at or before the pickup (a geofence re-entry on the way out is not a wait); MIN takes the first of possibly several arrivals. An order whose courier never logged an arrival drops out of the inner join: it has no measurable wait. The daypart is computed from the arrival converted to the merchant's zone; late night wraps midnight, so the CASE tests the hours before 06:00 explicitly and gives late night everything from 22:00. Orders cancelled before pickup never appear because the query starts from pickups.

Complexity. One sort for DISTINCT ON, one join on (order_id, courier_id) and a hash aggregate: O(n log n) over events. At scale, events are partitioned by order (or by date with the order's events co-located) so the whole computation is local per order before the final aggregate.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) works as written for TIMESTAMP; no DISTINCT ON (use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() …); COUNTIF. Snowflake: CONVERT_TIMEZONE(time_zone, arrived_at) then HOUR(…); QUALIFY, COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: from_utc_timestamp(arrived_at, time_zone) then hour(…). MySQL 8: CONVERT_TZ(arrived_at, '+00:00', time_zone) needs the time-zone tables loaded, otherwise it returns NULL; ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE, SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. A wait of exactly {{n_min}} minutes (not long) and one second over; an arrival at exactly 11:00 and at 17:00 local; an arrival in breakfast with the pickup in lunch; late-night arrivals after local midnight; a cancelled order with an arrival but no pickup; merchants in two time zones (one may be a half-hour offset). Hard: reassigned orders where another courier arrived earlier; a courier with two arrivals before the pickup. Very Hard: arrivals after the pickup; duplicated PICKED_UP rows; a pickup whose courier never logged an arrival while another courier did.

Common mistakes. Using the UTC hour; daypart from the pickup; the earliest arrival of any courier; the last arrival; >= for a long wait; BETWEEN 22 AND 6 (empty); the last PICKED_UP row; counting cancelled orders in orders; applying the floor before removing unmeasured orders; ordering dayparts alphabetically.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Log the merchant's "order ready" time and the dispatch's planned arrival time; split each wait into "arrived before ready" (dispatch) and "ready but not handed over" (merchant). (2) A spring-forward day has a 23-hour local day: the daypart containing the jump (usually late night) is an hour shorter; AT TIME ZONE with a zone name handles it, a fixed offset does not. (3) A high percentile per merchant and daypart, conditioned on basket size, with a minimum sample and shrinkage towards the city's value; the mean is pulled by rare extreme waits and hides the routine ones. (4) One arrival serves both orders: the wait belongs to the courier trip, not to each order; count it once per arrival (or split it) and keep orders as a separate count.

Rubric anchors. 2: plausible structure but wrong clock or wrong courier. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also separates merchant from dispatch causes and handles DST and batching credibly.

Strong signals. Asks which courier's wait counts and which clock the merchant uses before writing SQL; builds the daypart from the arrival on purpose. Red flags. Hard-coding a UTC offset; joining every arrival to every pickup and taking MAX − MIN.

def nearest_drivers(updates, requests, k, max_ring, claim=False):
    current = {}                                   # driver -> (q, r, status), last row wins
    for driver, q, r, status in updates:
        current[driver] = (q, r, status)
    cells = {}                                     # (q, r) -> sorted ids of open drivers there
    for driver, (q, r, status) in current.items():
        if status == 'open':
            cells.setdefault((q, r), []).append(driver)
    for ids in cells.values():
        ids.sort()

    directions = ((1, 0), (1, -1), (0, -1), (-1, 0), (-1, 1), (0, 1))
    get = cells.get
    out = []
    for q0, r0 in requests:
        found = list(get((q0, r0), ()))
        ring = 1
        while len(found) < k and ring <= max_ring:
            ring_ids = []
            q, r = q0 - ring, r0 + ring            # ring * direction 4, then walk the six sides
            for dq, dr in directions:
                for _ in range(ring):
                    ids = get((q, r))
                    if ids:
                        ring_ids.extend(ids)
                    q += dq
                    r += dr
            ring_ids.sort()
            found.extend(ring_ids)
            ring += 1
        found = found[:k]
        if claim and found:
            q, r, _ = current[found[0]]
            cell = cells[(q, r)]
            cell.remove(found[0])
            if not cell:
                del cells[(q, r)]
        out.append(found)
    return out

Explanation. Only each driver's last update matters, so the stream collapses into a dict first; the available drivers are then indexed by cell, each cell's ids sorted once. For a request, ring 0 is its own cell; ring d is the set of cells at exactly distance d, which the walk reaches by starting d steps along one direction (here (−1, +1)) and taking d steps along each of the six directions in turn. Every driver found in ring d is at distance exactly d, so sorting each ring's ids and appending rings in order produces the list in (distance, driver_id) order. As soon as a finished ring brings the list to k, no later ring can contribute, so the search stops. In claim mode the first driver of each non-empty list is removed from its cell's list (which stays sorted).

Complexity. Building the index is O(U + D log D). A request costs O(R² + c log c) for the R rings it needs (3R(R + 1) + 1 cells at most) and c drivers found, independent of the fleet size; at the timing test's density (about one available driver per five to ten cells) that is a few dozen cells per request. A scan of every available driver per request is O(Q × D), about 7 × 10⁸ distance computations in the timing test, which took over 100 seconds in CPython when checked (the reference: about half a second).

Common mistakes. max(|dq|, |dr|) or a Euclidean distance on axial coordinates; using the first update of a driver instead of the last; including on_trip or offline drivers; < instead of <= for max_ring; ties by numeric id or by insertion order; stopping in the middle of a ring once k are found (a later cell of the same ring can hold a smaller id); a BFS with a visited set that revisits cells or misses ring boundaries; forgetting to remove a claimed driver, or removing it only from the current request's list.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Use rings to get a few dozen candidates, then compute road ETAs for those only (a candidate-generation then re-ranking pattern), widening the rings when ETAs are poor. (2) An update is a remove from the old cell and an insert into the new one, O(cell size); shard by coarse cell with overlap (or route each request to the shards its rings touch), and keep each shard's index in memory. (3) Two riders and two drivers on a line: greedy gives the first rider the driver that the second needed and sends the second far away; batching requests over a short window and solving an assignment (Hungarian or min-cost flow) minimises total pickup distance at the cost of a little latency. (4) Search coarse cells first to find non-empty regions, then descend; or keep per-coarse-cell counts so empty areas are skipped in one step.

from bisect import bisect_right


def fares(trips, rates, surges):
    windows = sorted(surges)                     # half-open, never overlapping
    starts = [w[0] for w in windows]
    per_min, per_km = rates['per_minute'], rates['per_km']
    out = {}
    for trip_id, pings, tolls in trips:
        # Work in units of 1/300000 cent so every charge is an exact integer:
        # m/100 * (dt*per_min/60 + dm*per_km/1000) cents = m*(50*dt*per_min + 3*dm*per_km) units.
        units = rates['base'] * 300000
        high = pings[0][1]                       # odometer high-water mark
        for (t0, _), (t1, odo) in zip(pings, pings[1:]):
            i = bisect_right(starts, t0) - 1
            m = windows[i][2] if i >= 0 and t0 < windows[i][1] else 100
            dm = 0
            if odo > high:
                dm, high = odo - high, odo
            units += m * (50 * (t1 - t0) * per_min + 3 * dm * per_km)
        metered = (units + 150000) // 300000      # one rounding, half up (units >= 0)
        fare = max(metered, rates['minimum'])
        first, last = pings[0][0], pings[-1][0]
        charged = {}
        for toll_id, t, cents in tolls:
            if first <= t <= last and toll_id not in charged:
                charged[toll_id] = cents
        toll_cents = sum(charged.values())
        out[trip_id] = (fare, toll_cents, fare + rates['booking_fee'] + toll_cents)
    return out

Explanation. Money is kept in integers: multiplier_pct / 100 × (dt × per_minute / 60 + dm × per_km / 1000) cents equals multiplier_pct × (50·dt·per_minute + 3·dm·per_km) units of 1/300 000 cent, so every charge is an exact integer and the trip's total can be rounded once, halves up, with integer division. Windows are sorted once; bisect_right(starts, t) − 1 is the only window whose start is at or before t, and it contains t only if t is before its end (half-open). The odometer high-water mark makes a glitch that reads lower add nothing, and resumes distance from the highest reading so far (below Very Hard readings never decrease, so it is the plain difference). The minimum applies to the metered fare; the booking fee and tolls are added afterwards and never surged. Tolls are charged once per toll_id, only within the trip's first and last ping.

Common mistakes. Floats and round() (half to even, and binary fractions: round(202.5) == 202); rounding each interval; the multiplier from the interval's end, or windows closed at both ends; surging the base fare; adding tolls or the booking fee before the minimum; charging a retried toll twice; charging a toll crossed after the trip ended; negative distance from a glitch; measuring after a glitch from the glitch reading instead of the high-water mark (that charges the same metres twice); assuming surges is sorted.

(4) The lookup becomes per (cell, time); an interval that crosses cells needs a rule (start cell, or a split at the crossing), and the rule must be stated and versioned like any pricing rule.

def smooth_surge(cells, k, cap, prev=None, max_step=None, weighted=False):
    raw = {}
    for cell, (demand, supply) in cells.items():
        if demand <= supply:
            raw[cell] = 100
        elif supply == 0:
            raw[cell] = cap
        else:
            raw[cell] = min(cap, 100 * demand // supply)
    # every axial offset within hex distance k, with its weight
    ring = []
    for dq in range(-k, k + 1):
        for dr in range(max(-k, -dq - k), min(k, -dq + k) + 1):
            d = (abs(dq) + abs(dr) + abs(dq + dr)) // 2
            ring.append((dq, dr, k + 1 - d if weighted else 1))
    out = {}
    get = raw.get
    for (q, r) in cells:
        s = w = 0
        for dq, dr, wt in ring:
            v = get((q + dq, r + dr))
            if v is not None:
                s += wt * v
                w += wt
        v = (2 * s + w) // (2 * w)                 # round half up, in integers
        if prev is not None:
            p = prev.get((q, r), 100)
            v = min(max(v, p - max_step), p + max_step)
        out[(q, r)] = min(max(v, 100), cap)
    return out

Explanation. Three passes. First every raw multiplier, once. Then, for each cell, the fixed list of axial offsets within distance k (3k(k + 1) + 1 of them: 7 for k = 1, 19 for k = 2, 37 for k = 3), each one a dictionary lookup, summing weight × raw over the cells that have data. The average is rounded half up with integers only: (2S + W) // (2W). Finally the step limit around the previous value (100 when the cell is new), then the 100 and cap bounds. The offsets are generated by bounding dr so that |dq + dr| ≤ k, which gives each offset exactly once.

Complexity. O(N · k²) time for N cells, O(N) memory. The timing check is about 52 000 cells with k = 3: roughly 1.9 million lookups, under a second in CPython. Comparing every pair is about 2.7 billion distance checks.

Dialect notes. In SQL this is a self-join of the cell table to an offsets table (JOIN offsets o ON TRUE JOIN cells n ON n.q = c.q + o.dq AND n.r = c.r + o.dr) followed by GROUP BY c.q, c.r. In Spark the same join broadcasts the small offsets table. Libraries for real hexagonal indexes provide a "grid disk" or k-ring function that returns the neighbouring cell ids directly. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Demand equal to supply; no drivers with and without requests; truncation of the raw ratio; a raw ratio above the cap; (+1, −1) as a neighbour and (+1, +1) as not (the square-grid mistake); a cell exactly k away and one k + 1 away; an average of exactly half a hundredth; cells without data left out. At Hard: a rise and a fall limited by max_step, a move of exactly max_step, a cell missing from prev, and a previous value above the cap. At Very Hard: distance weights, and weights counted only for cells that have data.

Common mistakes. Chebyshev or Manhattan distance on (q, r), which picks the wrong six neighbours; treating missing cells as 1.00x; round() (half to even) or floats; capping before the step limit, so a cell whose previous value was above a lowered cap is held above it; applying the step to the raw value instead of the smoothed value; forgetting that the step limit starts from 100 for a new cell.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Weight the centre more, require a minimum number of drivers before a cell's own ratio is trusted, or blend the cell's value with the neighbourhood's by how much data it has; measure on replayed intervals how often a real spike is damped. (2) Keep the per-cell raw values and the k-ring sums; when a cell changes by Δ, add Δ × weight to the sums of the cells in its own k-ring, which is O(changed · k²). (3) The step limit slows oscillation but does not remove it; add hysteresis (only move when the change exceeds a threshold), smooth over time as well as space, and watch boundary crossings. (4) Shadow mode: compute the new rule beside the old one on live or replayed inputs, compare distributions and downstream metrics offline, then a limited experiment with guardrails.

def insert_rider(start, onboard, capacity, stops, pickup, dropoff,
                 max_wait, max_ride, seats=1, dwell=0):
    def dist(a, b):
        return abs(a[0] - b[0]) + abs(a[1] - b[1])

    n = len(stops)
    big = 1 << 62
    locs = [start] + [(s[2], s[3]) for s in stops]        # location 0 is the start
    dep = [0] * (n + 1)          # time the car leaves location i
    arr = [0] * (n + 1)          # time the car reaches location i
    load = [onboard] * (n + 1)   # seats taken when the car leaves location i
    slack = [big] * (n + 2)      # how late stop i may become
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        _rider, kind, _x, _y, latest, size = stops[i - 1]
        arr[i] = dep[i - 1] + dist(locs[i - 1], locs[i])
        dep[i] = arr[i] + dwell
        load[i] = load[i - 1] + (size if kind == "pickup" else -size)
        if latest is not None:
            slack[i] = latest - arr[i]
    suffix = [big] * (n + 2)     # min slack of stops i..n
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):
        suffix[i] = min(slack[i], suffix[i + 1])

    def gap(i, x):
        """Extra time to visit x between location i and location i + 1."""
        if i == n:
            return dist(locs[i], x) + dwell
        return dist(locs[i], x) + dwell + dist(x, locs[i + 1]) - dist(locs[i], locs[i + 1])

    best = None
    for i in range(n + 1):                       # the pickup goes right after location i
        if load[i] + seats > capacity:
            continue
        a_pick = dep[i] + dist(locs[i], pickup)
        if a_pick > max_wait:
            continue
        # drop-off immediately after the pickup
        a_drop = a_pick + dwell + dist(pickup, dropoff)
        if a_drop - a_pick <= max_ride:
            if i == n:
                added = dist(locs[i], pickup) + dwell + dist(pickup, dropoff) + dwell
            else:
                added = (dist(locs[i], pickup) + dwell + dist(pickup, dropoff) + dwell
                         + dist(dropoff, locs[i + 1]) - dist(locs[i], locs[i + 1]))
            if suffix[i + 1] >= added and (best is None or added < best[0]):
                best = (added, i, i + 1)
        if i == n:
            continue
        # drop-off right after a later stop j: stops i+1..j move by d1, the rest by d1 + d2
        d1 = gap(i, pickup)
        low = big
        for j in range(i + 1, n + 1):
            low = min(low, slack[j])
            if low < d1 or load[j] + seats > capacity:
                break                                 # every later j fails the same way
            a_drop = dep[j] + d1 + dist(locs[j], dropoff)
            if a_drop - a_pick > max_ride:
                break                                 # the ride only gets longer
            added = d1 + gap(j, dropoff)
            if suffix[j + 1] >= added and (best is None or added < best[0]):
                best = (added, i, j + 1)
    return best

Explanation. Precompute the plan once: arrival and departure time at each stop, the load when the car leaves each location (location 0 is the start), and each stop's slack latest − arrival, with suffix minima. A stop x inserted after location i delays every later stop by gap(i, x) = dist(i, x) + dwell + dist(x, i + 1) − dist(i, i + 1) (no last term at the end of the route). For a pickup after location i: the car must have room when it leaves i and the pickup must be on time. The drop-off can follow immediately, which shifts every later stop by one combined detour. Otherwise the drop-off goes after a later stop j: stops i + 1 … j move by d1 = gap(i, pickup) and need slack ≥ d1; stops after j move by d1 + gap(j, dropoff) and need suffix slack ≥ that; the rider is in the car when it leaves every stop from i to j, so those loads plus seats must fit. Walking j forward keeps a running minimum slack and checks loads one at a time; both conditions only get harder as j grows, so the loop can stop. The ride time also only grows with j (triangle inequality, dwell ≥ 0), so that check can stop the loop too. Scanning i and j in increasing order and keeping only strictly cheaper candidates gives the specified tie-break.

Complexity. O(n) precomputation and O(n²) pairs at most, each O(1); O(n) memory. The timing check is a 600-stop route: under 0.1 s for the reference, while simulating each of the ~180 000 candidate routes takes tens of seconds in CPython.

Dialect notes. Production dispatchers usually work with travel-time matrices from a routing engine rather than Manhattan distances, and check far fewer stops per car; the same prefix and suffix structure applies. In a JVM or C++ implementation the same algorithm is the norm, often with the outer loop over candidate drivers run in parallel. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. An idle driver; a rider exactly on the way (cost 0); equal costs everywhere (tie-break); a full car that can take the rider only after a drop-off; max_wait exactly and one second over (and None); max_ride exactly and one second over with no alternative (None); max_ride forcing the drop-off before another stop. At Hard: a promised stop reached exactly on time, one second late, and a tight promise late in the route. At Very Hard: a party of two that needs two seats for the whole ride, dwell at an inserted stop delaying a promised stop, and dwell at the pickup counted in the ride time.

Common mistakes. Checking capacity only at the pickup, or forgetting the load when the car leaves stop j; shifting every later stop by the full detour even when only the pickup has been inserted before them; forgetting the end-of-route case, where there is no "next" term; returning the old-sequence positions instead of the new ones; counting dwell at the start; checking latest on departure; using < at the boundaries; treating the triangle inequality as an assumption to prune by without saying so.

(1) Most time goes to travel-time lookups and to drivers that cannot work: filter by distance to the pickup, by free seats and by remaining slack before calling; cache travel times per request; stop early when a driver's lower bound on cost exceeds the best found. (2) The early exit on ride time used the triangle inequality; without it, keep checking the ride time for every j (still O(n²)) and make sure the detour formula uses the routing service's times consistently. (3) Serialise per vehicle: a conditional update on the vehicle's plan version (compare-and-set), so the second request is re-evaluated against the new plan. (4) Re-plan when insertions accumulate detours or a cheaper order exists; the promised times and the "no reordering of picked-up riders" rule constrain it, and re-planning is a local search or exact search only for small plans.

ALLOWED = {
    None: {"requested"},
    "requested": {"accepted", "cancelled"},
    "accepted": {"arrived", "cancelled"},
    "arrived": {"started", "cancelled"},          # a rider no-show is cancelled after arrival
    "started": {"completed"},
    "completed": set(),
    "cancelled": set(),
}
LIFECYCLE = {"requested", "accepted", "arrived", "started", "completed", "cancelled"}


def reconstruct_trips(events):
    by_trip = {}
    seen = set()
    for ev in events:
        evs = by_trip.setdefault(ev["trip"], [])
        if ev["event_id"] in seen:                   # a retransmitted copy
            continue
        seen.add(ev["event_id"])
        evs.append(ev)

    out = {}
    for trip, evs in by_trip.items():
        evs.sort(key=lambda ev: ev["seq"])           # the trip's order, not the phone's clock
        state, started_at, seconds, illegal = None, None, None, 0
        for ev in evs:
            t = ev["type"]
            if t not in LIFECYCLE:                   # location and other events: ignored
                continue
            if t not in ALLOWED[state]:
                illegal += 1
                continue                             # counted, never applied
            state = t
            if t == "started":
                started_at = ev["device_ts"]
            elif t == "completed":
                seconds = ev["device_ts"] - started_at
        out[trip] = {"state": state, "trip_seconds": seconds, "illegal": illegal}
    return out

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Ordered by the phone's clock. evs.sort(key=device_ts) mixes two phones' clocks. When the driver's phone runs slow, accepted sorts before requested, is illegal, and every later step is judged from the wrong state. Symptom: trips whose driver's clock is slow show up as never accepted, with high illegal counts. Fix: sort by seq.
  2. Retransmitted copies applied twice. There is no deduplication by event_id, so the second copy of accepted is an accepted → accepted transition and is counted as illegal. Symptom: illegal counts rise with network flakiness, not with real problems. Fix: drop events whose event_id has been seen.
  3. Illegal transitions applied. The code counts an illegal event but then sets state = t anyway (a missing continue). Symptom: a late cancel after completion turns a completed trip into a cancelled one; a stale accepted retry moves a trip backwards; a double-tapped start resets the start time. Fix: continue after counting.
  4. No cancel after arrival. The table has "arrived": {"started"}, so a rider no-show cancellation is illegal and the trip stays arrived. Symptom: no-show trips stuck in "arrived" for ever. Fix: allow cancelled from arrived.
  5. Location events counted. Every type that is not an allowed transition is counted as illegal, including location. Symptom: the illegal-event alarm tracks the location sampling rate. Fix: ignore types outside the lifecycle before the transition check.

Each bug has its own check that only it fails: a slow driver clock (1), a retransmitted copy (2), a stale accepted retry with a new id (3, also the double tap, the cancel after completion and the lost request), a no-show (4), and location events (5, also a trip with only location events). The reversed-delivery and two-trip checks pass on the original code because its phone clocks agree there: ordering by device time is wrong in general but right whenever the clocks agree, which is why bug 1 survives casual testing. Worth discussing with the candidate.

Explanation. A trip is a small state machine. The job must (a) collapse copies to one event, (b) order a trip's events by a sequence assigned in one place, (c) filter out events that are not part of the machine, and (d) apply only allowed transitions, counting the others. Durations are differences of timestamps from one phone, so a constant clock offset cancels; ordering across two phones has no such protection.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the per-trip sorts, O(n) memory for the groups and the seen-id set. The timing check is 200 000 events.

Dialect notes. In SQL the same rules are ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY …) = 1 for copies and an ordered fold over seq, which plain SQL expresses poorly: a recursive CTE, or MATCH_RECOGNIZE where the engine supports it (Snowflake, Oracle). In Spark, groupBy(trip) and a sorted fold per group (applyInPandas or flatMapGroupsWithState for streaming). Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Reverse delivery; a slow driver clock; a retransmitted copy; a stale retry with a new id; a no-show; location events; a double tap; a cancel after completion; a lost request; a trip with only location events; two trips interleaved.

Common mistakes. Fixing the sort but deduplicating on (trip, type), which also drops the double tap that should be counted; deduplicating after counting; adding continue but still updating started_at before the check; allowing a cancel from started, which the specification does not; raising an exception on an illegal transition; dropping trips with only location events from the output.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Emit a provisional state per trip when events arrive, with a version, and corrections as new versions; final states after a watermark plus a grace period; late events after that produce a correction record. Consumers read the latest version. (2) Bound the seen-id set by time: ids older than the longest retry window can be forgotten, or deduplicate per trip, keeping ids only until the trip is final plus a grace period. A copy arriving after that would be applied again, so the transition check must be safe for it, which it is for every terminal state. (3) Break down illegal counts by app version, platform and transition; a pipeline bug shows across all versions at once and around a deploy, an app bug follows the release's rollout. (4) Use the server's receipt time for the start and end events, or a monotonic elapsed-time counter from the phone, which a clock sync does not change; the cost is network delay in the server time, and support in the app for the monotonic counter.

UBR-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Scope. The affected set comes from data, not complaints: trips whose recorded rule version is one of the faulty releases, in the affected cities and vehicle class, within the window, plus a guard band before and after it. Every trip in scope is recomputed; the diff decides who is affected.
  • Recompute (pure). A replay service runs the same pricing code with the corrected rule version, reading only pinned inputs: the trip's stored pricing inputs (quote inputs for upfront trips; measured time and distance for metered trips), surge, promotions applied, tolls, taxes and currency rounding rules. Output per trip and component: (trip_id, incident_id, run_id, component, charged_minor, corrected_minor, currency). Runs are versioned; a re-run with revised rules is a new run_id, never an overwrite.
  • Validate the replay. First replay the trips with the original faulty rules: it must reproduce the charged amounts exactly. Any mismatch means the replay is not faithful (missing inputs, a code difference) and must be fixed before trusting the corrected run.
  • Diff and review. Aggregate the per-component differences by city, currency, direction (over or under) and size; sample trips for manual review; finance and city operations sign off on a frozen run_id.
  • Policy. Written down and owned: refund overcharges to riders; absorb undercharges (or not, if policy says otherwise); for upfront trips, compare with the quote the rider agreed to; driver earnings adjusted upward where they were underpaid and, typically, not clawed back; minimum thresholds per currency below which no adjustment is sent (with the totals still reported).
  • Exclusions. Trips already refunded in full, disputed, or adjusted since the trip are routed to a manual or reduced path. The adjustment amount is computed net of what has already been returned.
  • Apply (idempotent). One adjustment per (incident_id, trip_id, party) with that tuple as the idempotency key, sent through the normal payments and earnings APIs; a state table (pending → sent → confirmed | failed) is written before and after each call. Restarts resend only pending or unknown ones, and the downstream key makes a resend harmless. Notifications go out only after confirmation.
  • Audit and reconciliation. Originals are never changed. The ledger gets adjustment entries referencing the incident; totals by currency reconcile to the signed-off diff; the run manifest records rule versions, code version and inputs.

Competing designs to accept. Recompute inside the warehouse with the pricing logic re-implemented in SQL (acceptable only with the reproduce-the-original check, since two implementations drift); a streaming job that recomputes as trips are read; a per-city phased rollout of adjustments. Any is fine if recompute and apply are separated and keys are deterministic.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A replay that reads live rules or live surge; promotions that are a percentage of the fare (they must be recomputed, not copied); rounding per component vs on the total; currencies with zero or three decimal places; the payments API rate limit for {trips_affected} adjustments; notifications sent before money moves; a second incident on the same trips (the key includes the incident).

Incident guidance.

  • Differences in cities the bug never touched: the replay is not faithful. Stop, run the original rules and find the input or code difference (for example a rounding change, a promotion rule or a later tax table), fix the replay, and re-run; never adjust trips on an unexplained diff.
  • Restart resends 12 000 requests: the payments system rejected them as duplicate keys, which is the design working. Reconcile the state table with the downstream confirmations, mark them confirmed, and alert only on keys whose payload differs.
  • Support already refunded some trips: compute the adjustment net of refunds already issued; exclude full refunds; report the excluded set to support so that agents do not refund again from the other side.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Recompute the promotion from the corrected fare by its own rule (percentage, cap); the rider's adjustment is the difference in what they paid; the promotion budget's accounting changes too. (2) The state table and the idempotency keys say exactly what was sent; on restart, query downstream by key for anything pending and resume. (3) A new run_id with the re-corrected rules; diff run 2 against run 1; send only the deltas with keys that include the run or a revision number, or net them in one follow-up adjustment per trip. (4) Signed-off diff frozen by run_id, adjustments keyed and linked to it, ledger entries reconciled in totals and by sample. (5) Taxes recomputed from the corrected fare with the tax rules in effect at the trip time; adjustments carry tax components, and finance confirms reporting.

Rubric anchors. 2: an UPDATE of the fares table and a loop of refunds; no replay check; no idempotency. 3: pure recompute with pinned versions, a reviewed diff, idempotent adjustments with deterministic keys, originals kept. 4: also the reproduce-the-original validation, explicit owned policies (upfront vs metered, riders vs drivers, thresholds), exclusions for prior refunds and disputes, reconciliation to the ledger, and a revision path for a second correction.

Strong signals. Asks whether trips were upfront or metered before designing; proposes replaying the faulty rules first. Red flags. "Charge everyone the difference"; adjustments without keys; overwriting charged amounts.

UBR-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Polygon store. A table of polygon versions: (polygon_id, version, type, priority, city, geometry, effective_from, effective_to, published_at, change_reason, retroactive). Validation on publish: valid geometry, effective_from < effective_to, no unintended overlap within a type, and a diff against the previous version (area change, cells added and removed). A version is immutable once published.
  • Cell cover. For each polygon version, cover it with cells at a fixed resolution (a hexagonal or square hierarchical grid) and label each cell interior or boundary. Very large polygons are covered at a coarser resolution for interiors plus finer boundary cells. The cover table (cell, polygon_id, version, kind, effective_from, effective_to) is rebuilt only for changed polygons.
  • Join. Each trip point is mapped to its cell; join on the cell and on effective_from ≤ event_time < effective_to; interior matches are final, boundary matches run an exact point-in-polygon test. Pickups use the pickup time and drop-offs the drop-off time. Overlaps are resolved per type by priority, so a point can have one operating zone, one pricing zone and several geofences.
  • Boundaries and accuracy. A documented rule for points exactly on an edge (for example inclusive for the lower-priority side) and for low-accuracy points: keep the raw assignment and also record a distance to the boundary and the reported accuracy, so that downstream teams can apply an owned tolerance, rather than snapping silently.
  • Runs and late trips. The daily run processes trips by event date partitions, including late trips for older dates, and records in a run manifest which polygon versions it read. Output partitions are overwritten per event date; each row carries polygon_id, version and match_kind.
  • Corrections. A retroactive correction is a new version with an earlier effective_from and retroactive = true. Affected trips are found from the cells whose assignment changes (the symmetric difference of the old and new covers) and the dates in range, and only those partitions are reprocessed. Published reports either stay as published with an adjustment in the next period, or are restated, per the owner's policy; both versions of the assignment are kept.

Competing designs to accept. A spatial SQL engine with a spatial index and ST_Contains (fine at {daily_trips} if it partitions by city and prunes with bounding boxes); Spark with a broadcast cell cover; a geohash or S2 cover instead of hexagons. The choice of grid matters less than the interior/boundary split and the effective-dated versions.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Polygons with thousands of vertices making exact tests slow (simplify only for interior covering, never for the exact test; split very large polygons into tiles); skew when one city's airport receives a large share of points; joining with the latest polygons; invalid geometries or inverted effective intervals; late trips landing after a day was considered final; a correction that silently changes paid incentives.

Incident guidance.

  • A corrected airport boundary effective 45 days ago, incentives already paid: reprocess only the affected cells and dates, produce the old-versus-new assignment diff, and hand it to the incentive owners: paid amounts are not reversed by the pipeline; any adjustment is a business decision made with the diff. Report both versions.
  • An event geofence with effective-to before effective-from: the publish validation should have rejected it; add that check, fix the version, reprocess the event's dates, and alert when a geofence of an active event matches zero trips.
  • Late trips joined with today's polygons: the join must use the trip's own time; fix it, reprocess the late trips' event dates, and add a test with a polygon that changed between the trip date and the run date.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Symmetric difference of covers × the 60 days, reprocess those partitions, publish a diff and keep both versions; published reports follow the restatement policy. (2) Tile the polygon and use finer boundary cells so that only a small share of points need the exact test; precompute an edge index per boundary cell. (3) The rule is a written choice: pickup time for pickup-area geofences, request time for pricing; record which timestamp each assignment used. (4) Measure the distance-to-boundary distribution and accuracy; propose a tolerance with the airport operations owner; run both rules side by side before switching. (5) The same versioned cover table loaded into the request-time service; a daily reconciliation compares the two assignments and alerts on disagreement above a threshold.

Rubric anchors. 2: a nightly cross join with ST_Contains against the latest polygons; no versions. 3: effective-dated versions, cell cover with interior and boundary cells, trip-time joins, recorded versions. 4: also targeted reprocessing for retroactive corrections with a restatement policy, explicit boundary and accuracy rules, publish-time validation, and handling of very large polygons and skew.

Strong signals. Asks which timestamp decides the version; separates the business decision about restating paid reports from the pipeline mechanics. Red flags. Joining with today's polygons; snapping points silently; overwriting polygons in place.

UBR-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Trips and legs.
    • vehicle_trips (vehicle_trip_id, driver_id, vehicle_id, city_id, product, is_shared, started_at, ended_at, distance_m, duration_s, route_version): what the driver did.
    • rider_legs (leg_id, vehicle_trip_id, rider_id, request_id, pickup_at, dropoff_at, pickup_cell, dropoff_cell, status completed|cancelled_by_rider|cancelled_by_driver|no_show). A non-shared trip has one leg; a shared trip has one leg per rider. A leg may exist without a started vehicle trip (a cancellation that still carries a fee).
  • Rider money. fare_quotes (quote_id, request_id, price_version, currency, quoted_at) with fare_quote_components (quote_id, type, amount_minor), and rider_charge_lines (line_id, leg_id, type base|time|distance|dynamic_adjustment|booking_fee|toll|airport_surcharge|promotion|tax|tip|cleaning_fee|cancellation_fee|adjustment|refund, amount_minor signed, currency, reason_code, source quote|trip_end|support|tip|payment, created_at, effective_for_date). The upfront quote's components become lines at trip end; the final-price difference (destination change) is its own adjustment line with a reason. Lines are append-only; a receipt is "all lines for the leg at time t".
  • Driver money. driver_earning_lines (line_id, vehicle_trip_id or leg_id NULL, driver_id, type fare_share|surge_or_boost|toll_reimbursement|tip|cancellation_fee_share|adjustment|incentive, amount_minor, currency, created_at, statement_period_id). Earnings are on the vehicle trip (once), with a tip line linked to the leg it came from.
  • Currency. currencies (code, minor_unit_exponent) following ISO 4217 (0, 2 or 3); presentation divides by 10^exponent, storage never does. Conversion to a reporting currency uses a dated rate table and is done only in reporting views, with the rate date recorded.
  • Facts. fct_rider_charge_line and fct_driver_earning_line at line grain (append-only, partitioned by created date); fct_leg (one row per leg, accumulating: quoted, final and adjusted totals, tip total, closed flag) and fct_vehicle_trip (one row per vehicle trip: earnings totals, online-time attribution).
  • Definitions (one acceptable wording). Gross bookings = Σ rider charge lines excluding tips and taxes collected on behalf of authorities (and excluding tolls passed through, if finance treats them as pass-through), net of refunds, by the date of the leg. Take rate = (gross bookings − Σ driver earnings excluding tips and pass-throughs) ÷ gross bookings, per city and currency, converted only after the per-currency computation.
  • Late changes. Tips and adjustments are lines with their own created_at; the report for a closed month uses a "restatement" policy: either post them in the month they arrive (activity basis) or restate with a published delta. The tip share uses trip-date cohorts that are final after {{tip_window_days}} days.

Competing designs to accept. A single trip table with a leg table only for shared rides (if non-shared trips still get a leg row or a view makes the grain uniform). An event-sourced fare service whose events are the lines. A double-entry ledger with rider, driver, marketplace and tax-authority accounts per trip; strong if receipts and statements are projections of it.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. One fare column overwritten by adjustments; earnings stored per leg and summed for shared trips; tips inside revenue; floats for money; exponent assumptions; converting currencies before computing take rate; recomputing whole months for late tips at {{daily_trips}} trips a day (touch only legs with new lines).

Incident guidance.

  • Late tips update the fact row: the fact was mutable and statements were generated from a different source. Contain by freezing the closed month's published numbers; rebuild facts as append-only lines; reconcile Σ statement lines to warehouse lines per driver and period daily. The tips metric is cohort-based and labelled provisional for {{tip_window_days}} days.
  • Earnings counted per rider on shared trips: fan-out from joining legs to vehicle-trip earnings. Fix the dashboard to aggregate earnings at vehicle-trip grain before joining; add a test that Σ earnings in the mart equals Σ earning lines; at {{shared_share}} shared trips, quantify the inflation by city.
  • Zero-decimal currency divided by 100: an exponent assumption in code. Revert the pipeline, recompute the affected days, read the exponent from the currency table, and add a per-currency anomaly check (day-over-day gross bookings within a band) so a small market's hundredfold drop alerts.

Follow-up guidance. (1) One vehicle trip, three legs, each with its own lines; the destination change is an adjustment line on that rider's leg; the driver statement has one set of earnings for the vehicle trip. (2) A tip line with created_at in the open month; the closed month's published total does not change; the cohort metric for the trip date updates and is labelled. (3) Tips, taxes and pass-through tolls excluded from gross bookings; refunds subtracted. (4) The take rate for that trip falls (rider paid less, driver paid the same); finance usually wants it, but reports it with the reason. (5) Lines at line grain; legs and vehicle trips as accumulating facts rebuilt only for touched keys.

Rubric anchors. 2: one trips table with fare and tip columns updated in place; shared rides as duplicated trips. 3: vehicle trip and leg grains, typed lines for rider and driver money, append-only adjustments, integer minor units, written definitions. 4: also currency exponents and dated conversion, late-tip policy for closed months, fan-out prevention for shared trips, and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Separates what the driver did from what each rider bought before drawing money tables; asks whether tips count as revenue. Red flags. Editing receipts; summing currencies; earnings per leg.

UBR-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Requirements. requirement_rules (rule_id, city_id, product, document_type, version, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, renewal_months NULL, grace_days, transition_until NULL, applies_to new|all). Rules are versioned; a change ends one version and starts another. A correction of an erroneous rule is a new version with the same valid time and a later recorded_at (bitemporal), so an audit can ask either question.
  • Documents. documents (document_id, driver_id, document_type, submitted_at, storage_ref); the image sits in an access-controlled object store with encryption and retention; document_fields (document_id, field, value, extracted_by ocr|reviewer, confidence, recorded_at); document_decisions (decision_id, document_id, decision approved|rejected|revoked, reason_code, decided_by automated|reviewer_id, decided_at, effective_from). Decisions are append-only; the latest by decided_at wins.
  • Compliance intervals. compliance_intervals (driver_id, city_id, product, valid_from, valid_to, status compliant|grace|blocked, cause rule_id/document_id, computed_at). Derived per driver by walking the effective rule set and the approved documents' validity (approval effective_from → expiry end instant, where expiry is the end of the printed date in the city's local time). Grace of {{grace_days}} days produces a grace interval. Recomputed on any event that touches the driver (document decision, rule version in their city) and nightly as a safety net.
  • Two time axes. Each interval set carries computed_at; "known then" is the set computed before the trip, "known now" is the latest. A revocation creates new intervals (and a list of affected trips) without deleting the old computation.
  • Facts. fct_onboarding_funnel (one row per driver and city: signed_up_at, docs_submitted_at, approved_at, first_trip_at); fct_document_review (one row per decision); fct_expiring_documents (daily snapshot); and the audit view joining trips to intervals with valid_from <= trip_started_at < valid_to.
  • Privacy. The warehouse holds document metadata and decisions, not images or document numbers in clear; deletion after the retention period removes personal fields and keeps pseudonymous audit facts (driver key, intervals, decisions) as policy allows.

Competing designs to accept. Computing compliance at query time from rules and documents (correct but slow; acceptable if they materialise the result for the online check). An event-sourced driver profile with projections. A rules engine owning requirement logic, with the warehouse storing its versioned outputs.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A boolean is_compliant flag; rules edited in place; expiry in server time; deleting rejected or revoked decisions; recomputing every driver nightly at {{drivers}} drivers across {{cities}} cities instead of on events; images copied into the warehouse.

Incident guidance.

  • Rule edited in place: restore the previous rule version from the change log or backups, re-add the correction as a new version, recompute intervals for the affected city, and rerun the audit. Guardrail: rule tables accept only inserts (permissions and a database trigger), and every audit cites the rule version.
  • Expiry evaluated in UTC: compute the expiry instant from the printed date in the city's time zone; list trips that ran between the true block time and the actual one, notify the safety team, and add a test with cities on both sides of UTC. With a {{grace_days}}-day grace, compute grace from the same local instant.
  • Day and month swapped by extraction: identify documents whose extracted date is ambiguous (both parts ≤ 12) for formats that use day/month; send them to review; block or unblock as the corrected date requires; store the document format with the extractor's output and add a confidence threshold below which a reviewer must confirm. Report the share per document type out of {{document_types}}.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Intervals: compliant until expiry, grace for {{grace_days}} days, blocked until renewal approval, compliant again, and a new blocked interval if the inspection requirement starts before an inspection is approved (or a transition interval if one applies). (2) Known-then report unchanged; known-now report lists the affected trips with the revocation as the cause. (3) A rule version with transition_until; intervals for existing drivers stay compliant until then. (4) Event-driven recomputation per driver; nightly sweep for expiries crossing midnight in each city's time zone. (5) Delete images and personal fields; keep pseudonymous intervals and decisions for the safety-audit retention period.

Rubric anchors. 2: a drivers table with document columns and an is_compliant flag. 3: versioned rules, append-only decisions, derived intervals, trips joined by time. 4: also bitemporal known-then/known-now, local-time expiry, transitions and revocations, privacy separation and event-driven recompute.

Strong signals. Asks how a past trip is audited before designing; treats expiry as a local-time instant. Red flags. Overwriting rules; deleting rejected documents; images in the warehouse.

UBR-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Grid. Cells are computed by the grid library, not stored as polygons: cell_id (64-bit index), resolution, and the library's parent function. A small cells table may be materialised only for cells in service areas, with the parent at the coarser resolutions in use. Parent relationships are by the library's definition; a coarser cell is not the exact union of its children, so area statistics at coarser resolutions are approximate.
  • Zone catalogue. zones (zone_id, type city|pricing|airport_pickup|event|tax, city_id, owner, precedence); zone_id survives redraws.
  • Zone versions. zone_versions (zone_version_id, zone_id, geometry, valid_from, valid_to NULL, recorded_at, author, reason, supersedes_version_id NULL). Immutable. Event geofences require a non-null valid_to. A split ends the old zone's version and starts versions of two zones, with a zone_lineage (from_zone_id, to_zone_id, at) table for continuous series.
  • Mapping. cell_zone_map (zone_version_id, cell_id, coverage center|partial) at the base resolution {{base_resolution}}, computed when a version is published (a polyfill by cell centre, plus boundary cells flagged partial). Lookup for pricing: point → cell id (library) → equality join to the map filtered by valid time and precedence; cached per city in memory.
  • Exact tests. Only for rules that require them (airport pickup queues, tax boundaries): if a point's cell is flagged partial for such a zone, run point-in-polygon against the version geometry.
  • Points. Each assigned point stores its cell id at the base resolution and, for facts, the zone_version_id used; re-assignment under "as it is" uses the cell id, never the raw coordinates again unless an exact test is needed.
  • Reporting. "As it was" uses the version in force at event time (default); "as it is" re-assigns history to the current versions, labelled; zone_lineage supports trends across splits.

Competing designs to accept. Storing polygons only and assigning by spatial index (R-tree) point-in-polygon at query time, if they address cost at {{daily_points}} points a day. Mapping at a finer resolution only near boundaries (compact cell sets). Geohash or S2 instead of hex cells, with a reasoned trade-off (exact nesting and prefix scans versus uniform neighbour distances).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Overwriting geometries; backdated versions silently rewriting closed months; coarser-parent rollups treated as exact; event geofences without an end; exact polygon tests on every point; mapping size explosion when moving to a finer resolution (about seven times the cells per step).

Incident guidance.

  • Backdated redraw re-assigned last month: valid time and recorded time were not separated, and the reassignment job was allowed to touch closed months. Restore the published month from the "as recorded" view, publish any restatement explicitly, and require approval for valid_from earlier than recorded_at, with an automatic list of affected reports.
  • Parent rollups double-count or miss edge trips: assign each trip to a zone at the base resolution {{base_resolution}} (or exactly), then aggregate by zone; use coarser cells only for display. Add a check that Σ zone totals equals the city total within the expected tolerance.
  • Event geofence without an end: require valid_to for event types, alert on events active longer than their declared window, and make the edit log searchable by zone type and author so one change among {{zone_edits_per_week}} a week is found in minutes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Old zone version ends; two new zones start; lineage rows link them; the trend shows the old zone until the split and the sum of the two after, labelled. (2) Pricing uses the cell's mapping (centre rule); the airport rule runs an exact test because the cell is flagged partial. (3) Cells ≈ city area ÷ average cell area at that resolution; one resolution finer is about seven times as many rows. (4) Facts that used the affected cells and dates are recomputed under a restatement; consumers are notified via a published change record. (5) At ingestion, with the cell id and zone_version_id stored on the point.

Rubric anchors. 2: one zones table with geometry overwritten; zone = set of cells assumed exact. 3: catalogue and immutable versions with valid time, a precomputed cell mapping, precedence, an exact test where needed. 4: also recorded time versus valid time, the approximate hierarchy handled correctly, lineage across splits and a backdating policy.

Strong signals. Asks how analysts compare a zone across a redraw; knows that children do not nest exactly. Red flags. Point-in-polygon for every point at scale; editing geometry in place; event geofences with no end time.

UBR-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Orders. orders (order_id, customer_id, merchant_id, city_id, placed_at, currency, ready_at, delivered_at); order_items (order_item_id, order_id, merchant_item_id, menu_version_id, item_name_snapshot, unit_price_minor, qty, substitution_preference); order_item_modifiers (order_item_id, modifier_name_snapshot, price_minor); picking_events (order_item_id, kind found|substituted|out_of_stock, qty, substitute_item_id NULL, at). A substitution is a delivered line linked to the ordered line, so both "ordered" and "sent" survive.
  • Menu. merchant_items (merchant_item_id, merchant_id), menu_versions (menu_version_id, merchant_id, published_at), menu_item_versions (menu_version_id, merchant_item_id, name, price_minor). Reports group by a platform-assigned stable item key; a reused merchant id with a different dish gets a new stable key (detected by name/category change at publish).
  • Dispatch. courier_trips (courier_trip_id, courier_id, started_at, ended_at, distance_m, status), trip_stops (courier_trip_id, seq, order_id, kind pickup|dropoff, arrived_at, departed_at). An order re-assigned after a courier cancels has stops on two trips; the completed one is marked.
  • Money lines. customer_charge_lines (order_id, order_item_id NULL, type item|modifier|delivery_fee|service_fee|small_order_fee|promotion|tip|tax, amount_minor, funder marketplace|merchant NULL); merchant_payout_lines (merchant_id, order_id, type item_sales|commission|promotion_merchant_funded|refund_merchant_liable|adjustment, amount_minor, payout_period_id); courier_pay_lines (courier_trip_id, type distance|time|extra_stop|incentive|tip, amount_minor) stored once per trip.
  • Refunds. refund_lines (refund_line_id, order_item_id, qty, amount_minor, reason missing|wrong|damaged|late, liable merchant|marketplace, channel app|support, idempotency_key, created_at), with a database check (or a guarded write path) that Σ qty ≤ ordered qty and Σ amount ≤ charged for the item; the idempotency key is (order_item_id, reason, request id from the channel).
  • Facts. fct_order_item (item grain: ordered, delivered, substituted, refunded qty and amounts, stable item key); fct_order (order grain: totals, ready-to-dropoff minutes, batched flag, allocated courier cost); fct_courier_trip (trip grain: pay, stops, distance). Courier cost per order = trip pay allocated by a stated rule (for example by each order's share of stop-to-stop distance, or equal per drop-off), computed once in fct_order with the rule name.
  • Visibility. Merchants see item, order and payout facts for their own orders; courier pay stays out of merchant views; couriers lose access to customer details after drop-off.

Competing designs to accept. Order-level money with item-level refunds only (if refund invariants still hold per item). A delivery ledger with accounts for customer, merchant, courier and marketplace. Allocating courier cost by time rather than distance, if the rule is written and consistent.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Joining courier pay to orders (fan-out); item names joined from the current menu; refunds without per-item invariants or idempotency; one delivery time for all audiences; courier per order modelled as a column (cannot represent batches or re-assignment); at {{daily_orders}} orders a day, rebuilding item facts nightly in full instead of touching orders with new refunds.

Incident guidance.

  • Courier pay counted per order on batched trips: aggregate pay at trip grain and allocate it; correct the dashboard and recompute history; add a check that Σ allocated cost = Σ trip pay per day. At {{batched_share}} batched orders the inflation is large; quantify it for the people who acted on the dashboard.
  • Reused item ids: snapshot names and prices on the order item; assign stable item keys at menu publish and detect reuse (name/category change); recompute refund rates on the stable key.
  • Double refunds from two channels: stop the second channel's automatic refunds, list items where Σ refunded > charged, reverse the excess (and the merchant payout deductions) with compensating lines, and enforce the invariant and an idempotency key in the refund write path. Against a normal {{refund_share}} of orders refunded, alert when the daily share jumps.

Follow-up guidance. (1) One trip, four stops, two orders; one refund line on the second order's item with liable party; cost per order from the allocation rule. (2) Stable item key plus name snapshot; old dish's history unaffected. (3) Check in the refund service before commit; a refund that would break it is rejected or routed to review. (4) A rule based on stops or distance; batching lowers cost per order if the allocation is honest. (5) Item grain for refunds and menu analytics, order grain for delivery time and cost, trip grain for pay; late refunds update only touched orders.

Rubric anchors. 2: orders with a courier_id column and an items array; refunds at order level. 3: item grain with snapshots, many-to-many trips and orders via stops, typed money lines, item refunds with invariants. 4: also allocation rule, stable item keys against reuse, idempotent refunds across channels, audience-specific delivery times and visibility rules.

Strong signals. Sees the many-to-many between trips and orders immediately; asks who bears each refund. Red flags. Joining to the current menu for history; summing trip pay over orders; refunds without a cap per item.

UBR-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{report_date}} and {{min_requests}} are the instance's values)

WITH req AS (
  SELECT r.request_id,
         r.city_id,
         date_trunc('hour', r.requested_at AT TIME ZONE c.time_zone) AS local_hour,
         COALESCE(w.multiplier, 1.00) > 1.00 AS surged
  FROM ride_requests r
  JOIN cities c ON c.city_id = r.city_id
  LEFT JOIN surge_windows w
         ON w.zone_id = r.zone_id
        AND w.starts_at <= r.requested_at
        AND r.requested_at < w.ends_at
  WHERE (r.requested_at AT TIME ZONE c.time_zone)::date = DATE '{{report_date}}'
), completed AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT request_id
  FROM trips
  WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT q.city_id,
       q.local_hour,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS requests,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE q.surged)             AS surged_requests,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE q.surged)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS request_surge_share,
       COUNT(d.request_id)                          AS completed_trips,
       COUNT(d.request_id) FILTER (WHERE q.surged)  AS surged_completed_trips,
       ROUND(COUNT(d.request_id) FILTER (WHERE q.surged)::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(d.request_id), 0), 4)   AS completed_surge_share
FROM req q
LEFT JOIN completed d ON d.request_id = q.request_id
GROUP BY q.city_id, q.local_hour
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_requests}}
ORDER BY q.city_id, q.local_hour;

Explanation. Each request is priced first: a LEFT JOIN to its zone's windows with the half-open condition starts_at <= requested_at < ends_at finds at most one window (windows of a zone never overlap), and a request with no window keeps a NULL multiplier that COALESCE turns into 1.00. Surge is strictly above 1.00, so explicit 1.00x windows and requests outside every window are unsurged but stay in the denominator. Trips are reduced to the set of request ids with a completed trip before the join, so a re-matched request (driver-cancelled trips before the final one) is still one row. AT TIME ZONE converts a timestamptz to the city's wall-clock time; the hour and the report date both come from it. A completed trip is attributed to its request's row, so it counts in the request's hour whenever it ended. COUNT(d.request_id) counts only matched (completed) rows; NULLIF makes the share NULL for an hour with nothing completed. The floor is a HAVING on the request count.

Complexity. One pass over the day's requests with an index or sort-merge range join on (zone_id, starts_at) for windows, a hash of completed request ids, and one hash aggregate by (city, hour). In production the request's quoted multiplier is stored with the request when it is priced, which removes the range join altogether; the date filter becomes a UTC range per city (local midnight to local midnight) so partitions on requested_at can be pruned.

Dialect notes. Time zones: Snowflake CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', c.time_zone, requested_at) (or CONVERT_TIMEZONE(c.time_zone, requested_at) for a TIMESTAMP_TZ), then DATE_TRUNC('hour', …); BigQuery DATETIME_TRUNC(DATETIME(requested_at, c.time_zone), HOUR); Spark SQL date_trunc('hour', from_utc_timestamp(requested_at, c.time_zone)); MySQL 8 CONVERT_TZ(requested_at, '+00:00', c.time_zone), which needs the server's time-zone tables loaded. Filtered counts: Snowflake COUNT_IF(…), BigQuery COUNTIF(…), Spark SQL supports FILTER (WHERE …) and count_if, MySQL SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Division by zero: BigQuery SAFE_DIVIDE returns NULL; Snowflake's DIV0 and DIV0NULL return 0, not NULL, so use NULLIF there. ROUND rounds half away from zero on exact decimals in these engines, but BigQuery's / returns FLOAT64, so cast to NUMERIC before rounding if exact ties matter. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A surged window hit by one request exactly at starts_at (surged) and one exactly at ends_at (not priced by it); a window that sets exactly 1.00x with a request inside; a request exactly on a local hour; requests on the neighbouring local days (before local midnight of the report date, and from local midnight of the next day, sometimes exactly at it); an hour whose requests have no completed trip (NULL share); completed trips that end in a later hour. Hard adds re-matched requests (one or more driver-cancelled trips before the final trip), adjacent windows of one zone with different multipliers, and a minimum-requests floor with an hour below it. Very Hard adds three cities including one at UTC+5:30, and an hour 0 with a request exactly at local midnight and another one second before it.

Common mistakes. Bucketing hours or filtering the date in UTC; BETWEEN on the window (end inclusive: double counting with adjacent windows); an exclusive start; an inner join to windows (unsurged requests vanish); >= 1.00 as surge; counting completed trips in their end hour; dividing surged completions by all requests; 0 instead of NULL for an empty denominator; (Hard+) joining requests to all trips before counting, and forgetting the floor. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Compute day-level shares from summed counts (Σ surged ÷ Σ requests); an average of hourly shares weights a quiet hour like a busy one. (2) Use the quoted multiplier stored on the request (or a price_quotes table keyed by request) as the record of what the rider saw; windows describe intent and can be corrected. (3) Truncating a local timestamp merges both occurrences of the repeated hour into one row (twice the usual requests); the report should label it or key hours by UTC offset as well; on a spring-forward day the missing hour has no row. (4) Store the multiplier at pricing time; partition requests by UTC date and city; compute per city-hour incrementally from a stream with late-event handling, keyed by local hour.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape, but UTC hours or a fan-out through trips or an inner join to windows. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains summed-count rollups, storing the quoted multiplier, and repeated local hours.

Strong signals. Asks which time zone defines a city's day before writing SQL; reduces trips to one flag per request without being told. Red flags. BETWEEN for time windows; averaging hourly shares; hard-coding UTC offsets per city.
UBR-L3-05.reference_sql:
WITH req AS (
  SELECT r.request_id,
         r.city_id,
         date_trunc('hour', r.requested_at AT TIME ZONE c.time_zone) AS local_hour,
         COALESCE(w.multiplier, 1.00) > 1.00 AS surged
  FROM ride_requests r
  JOIN cities c ON c.city_id = r.city_id
  LEFT JOIN surge_windows w
         ON w.zone_id = r.zone_id
        AND w.starts_at <= r.requested_at
        AND r.requested_at < w.ends_at
